# On the Peculiar Comfort of Unfinished Things

I've been thinking lately about incompleteness, and how we've developed such an anxious relationship with it. Not the incompleteness of failure—that's a different animal entirely—but the everyday incompleteness that characterizes most of life. The book with a bookmark three-quarters through. The half-written email in a draft folder. The skill you're learning that may never make you exceptional. The thought you had yesterday that you never quite articulated.

We live in an age of completion culture. Everything must be finished, shipped, monetized, published, optimized. The work-in-progress is only valuable insofar as it becomes a finished product. An artist's sketches matter mainly because they lead to the gallery painting. Notes are only important if they eventually become the book. We've been taught that the unfinished is the unsuccessful, the abandoned, the failed.

But I wonder if we're missing something.

There's a specific kind of freedom in incompleteness that completion destroys. When something is finished, it becomes fixed. The sculpture is cast. The painting is varnished. The sentence is published. And in that fixing comes a certain closure that is both satisfying and suffocating. You can't change it anymore. You can't add to it or reshape it. It exists as it is, forever, which is wonderful until you realize you'd do it differently now.

The unfinished, by contrast, remains alive with possibility. It can become anything. The character sketch that never grew into a full story still contains infinite potential versions of that character. The sketch of the landscape still could become a painting, a photograph, a poem, or just remain a sketch that someone finds twenty years later and sees something entirely new in. There's something almost sacred about that openness.

I think about my grandmother's knitting basket—she'd started at least fifteen projects that she never completed. Some of them were just a few inches of fabric in progress. For years, my mother felt like these were failures, loose threads marking my grandmother's incomplete efforts. But toward the end of my grandmother's life, my mother understood something different: my grandmother hadn't abandoned these projects because she was lazy or incapable. She had simply moved on. She was interested in other things. And importantly, if someone she loved needed a scarf, she could pull out one of these partially-finished projects and complete it with specific intention, rather than making something new. The unfinished wasn't wasteful—it was flexible. It was resourceful. It was available.

There's also something honest about incompleteness. A finished thing must pretend to totality. It must suggest: "This is complete. This is what I meant to say. This is the full expression of the idea." But anyone who has ever finished something knows this is a lie we tell ourselves. Every finished work is really just a version that got interrupted by the need to call it done. Every book ends because the author ran out of time or funding or patience, not because the idea was actually exhausted. Every movie has deleted scenes. Every essay could go deeper.

The unfinished, though, admits its own limitations. It says: "This is as far as I got. There is more, but I'm showing you this." There's a peculiar honesty in that.

I'm also fascinated by the unfinished as a form of generosity. Some of the most beautiful and productive moments in human culture have come from incomplete things. The reader brings their own imagination to fill the gaps. A sketch can contain more power than a finished painting because the viewer must complete it in their mind. Hemingway wrote about the iceberg principle—that the power of writing comes from leaving most of it underwater, forcing readers to sense the whole. Incompleteness, in other words, can be a sophisticated artistic choice rather than a failure of execution.

There's also the temporal aspect I keep returning to. Everything in life is technically incomplete until we die, and even then, the impact and meaning of our lives continues to unfold for those we've affected. We're all unfinished works. Recognizing this is either terrifying or liberating depending on your mood, but I increasingly think it's supposed to be liberating.

If you accept that you're unfinished, you stop waiting for permission to exist. You don't need to be "ready" because readiness is a myth we tell ourselves. The person who waits until they're completely prepared, completely educated, completely confident never moves. But the person who accepts they'll always be somewhat unprepared, still learning, and not entirely sure—that person can actually do things.

I watched a musician once say that they never feel ready to perform. They perform anyway. The readiness, they said, would never come. So they had to choose: wait for something that wouldn't arrive, or proceed into incompleteness and find meaning in the attempt anyway. The incompleteness wasn't a failure of their preparation; it was the actual condition of performing, and accepting it made all the difference.

Maybe that's what we need to remember about our unfinished days, our incomplete projects, our partial ideas. They're not failures in waiting. They're the actual texture of a life lived, a mind engaged, a hand that tries even when it's not sure it will succeed.

I'm going to stop writing now, even though I could continue. There are more ideas forming at the edges of my mind—something about how unfinished conversations can sometimes matter more than resolved ones, something about the way paintings in museums have their own unfinished sections that we walk past without noticing. There are connections I haven't drawn, implications I haven't explored.

But maybe that's perfect. This piece is unfinished, and in its unfinishedness, it invites you to finish it in your own mind. To find what applies to your own unfinished things, whatever they might be. To sit with the uncomfortable idea that completion might not be the goal after all—that engagement with the incomplete, the partial, the still-becoming might be enough.

More than enough. Everything.
